item.title: Efficient MPO Construction for Long-Range Hamiltonians with Periodic Boundary Conditions: Application to Many-Body Dynamics
item.description:
Worth a look new method — MPO bond dimension scales as Drchain=r+2 under OBC and Drring=r2+3r+42 under PBC by embedding finite-range periodic channels directly into an open-boundary MPO, yielding average TDVP relative error of 0.58% for occupation and under 1.5% for correlations against RK4.

Grade 0.338 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “tensor network and matrix product state methods, and classical simulability of…” · Xin Wang, Bo Xiong

Figure

Time evolution and relative errors of average occupation n and spatial correlations Cr (r=1,2,3) comparing TDVP to RK4 under a quench protocol up to 0.7 μs. Relative error stays below 1% for occupation and below 5% for correlations across all interaction ranges.

Asks

How can compact MPOs incorporating both periodic boundary conditions and finite-range interactions be constructed for stable TDVP time evolution without breaking canonical gauge?

Before

was maximum bond dimension scaling as 2r for interaction range r in TEBD-based MPOs constructed from nonlocal exponentials

But

Spin-1/2 chain quench dynamics simulation over 0.7 μs, benchmarked up to third-nearest neighbors (r=3) and system sizes up to N=24.

Tools

matrix product operators · time-dependent variational principle · fourth-order Runge-Kutta benchmark

Abstract

Matrix product operator (MPO) serves as a fundamental component in tensor network simulations of quantum many-body dynamics. We employ an MPO construction that introduces additional propagation channels to embed both periodic boundary conditions and finite-range couplings directly into an open boundary MPO. We apply this construction within the time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) framework to simulate quench dynamics in a spin-1/2 chain with finite-range interactions, and benchmark the results numerically against the fourth-order Runge-Kutta method, finding excellent agreement for both single-body and two-body observables. The approach offers a practical route for tensor network simulations of many-body dynamics in periodic finite-range systems.

item.title: Pauli-string grouping for VQE measurement reduction on a sparse-connectivity quantum annealer
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Only H2 embeds onto current quantum annealing hardware for VQE Pauli-string grouping; all other molecular instances exceed the 4800-qubit Zephyr Z12 graph by factors between 23 and 2.0×105, with BeH2 under full commutativity requiring at least a Z59 topology (>105 physical qubits).

Grade 0.321 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum chemistry and electronic structure on quantum computers” · Raul Martinez, Miguel Sanchez-Beato, Mario Calonge

Figure

Compares grouping quality (number of Pauli groups) and computational cost (wall-clock time) for molecular Hamiltonians under full commutativity across classical heuristics and D-Wave solvers.

Asks

What is the physical-qubit embedding overhead, scalability limit, and practical performance of the Pauli-grouping colouring QUBO on a sparse-connectivity quantum annealer compared to classical heuristics?

Before

Small-scale colouring QUBO implementations on D-Wave processors exhibited rapid decay of valid samples with variable count (Jattana et al., 2023), but without characterizing the minor-embedding overhead or hardware graph capacity limits.

But

Evaluated on six molecular Hamiltonians in the STO-3G basis using Bravyi-Kitaev mapping and standard one-hot QUBO formulation. Compared against classical greedy heuristics rather than exact solvers.

Tools

D-Wave Advantage2_system1 (Zephyr topology) · D-Wave Leap Hybrid BQM solver · One-hot Minimum Vertex Colouring QUBO · Degree-counting minor-embedding lower bounds · Classical graph colouring heuristics (LF, RLF, Degree-Based)

Abstract

The Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) requires a large number of measurements to evaluate molecular Hamiltonians. Expressing a molecular Hamiltonian as a linear combination of Pauli strings creates a measurement bottleneck: non-commuting Pauli strings cannot be measured simultaneously. Consequently, mutually commuting Pauli strings must be grouped and measured together to minimise the number of quantum-state preparations. This task maps to the minimum clique cover problem on a commutativity graph, an NP-hard problem typically addressed using classical heuristics. Although an Ising-model formulation has recently been explored on fully connected CMOS Ising machines and demonstrated on physical quantum annealers only at small scale, the embedding cost that governs its behaviour on hardware with sparse connectivity, where each logical variable must be represented by a chain of physical qubits, has not been characterised. In this work, we formulate the Pauli-grouping problem as a standard QUBO colouring model and study its scalability on a D-Wave quantum annealer. Across a series of molecular systems and for both qubit-wise and full commutativity, we quantify the growth in the number of logical variables and the QUBO interaction density, characterise the physical-qubit and chain-length overhead required for embedding on the Zephyr topology, and compare the annealer's time-to-solution and solution quality with those of heuristic classical baselines. This analysis identifies the threshold of molecular complexity beyond which hardware connectivity prevents viable embedding, and shows that a second, practical limit is reached earlier. The threshold therefore measures how far current annealers are from the regime in which pre-optimising a VQE measurement scheme on hardware would be worth considering.

item.title: Time rescaling for second-order feedback-based quantum optimization
item.description:
Long shot new method — Unifying time-rescaling with second-order feedback in FALQON (TR-Hy-FALQON) reaches the Goemans-Williamson approximation ratio threshold rGW in 19 layers for 12-vertex 3-regular graphs and 13 layers for 14-vertex Erdős–Rényi graphs (p=0.3), yielding 40-layer approximation ratios of 0.968 and 0.966.

Grade 0.300 · 1.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum chemistry and electronic structure on quantum computers” · Leticia Bertuzzi, João P. Engster, Evandro C. R. da Rosa, Eduardo I. Duzzioni

Figure

Approximation ratio as a function of quantum circuit layers across FALQON variants and QAOA on 12-vertex 3-regular graphs and 14-vertex Erdős–Rényi graphs, comparing 30-instance averages against single-instance runs.

Asks

Can time-rescaled dynamics and second-order feedback laws be merged into a unified FALQON framework to reduce circuit depth without classical optimization?

Before

SO-FALQON required 32 layers for 3-regular graphs and 19 layers for Erdős–Rényi graphs to reach rGW, while TR-FALQON failed to reach rGW within 40 layers on 3-regular graphs and took 24 layers on Erdős–Rényi graphs.

But

Numerical simulations; tested on 12-vertex 3-regular graphs and 14-vertex Erdős–Rényi graphs (p=0.3) for the MaxCut problem; capped hybrid switching between second- and first-order update rules.

Tools

Feedback-based Algorithm for Quantum Optimization (FALQON) · Quantum Lyapunov control · Time-rescaling dynamics · Second-order energy expansion

Abstract

Feedback-based quantum algorithms recently gained attention by demonstrating how quantum computers can be used to solve optimization problems without resorting to hybrid quantum-classical architectures. Recent progress made with Feedback-based Algorithm for Quantum Optimization (FALQON) variants significantly reduced the depth of the required circuits. In this work, we merge the time-rescaled and second-order FALQON variants into a unified framework. The results show an important improvement over past modifications, reducing circuit depth and allowing a more flexible choice of time-steps, while maintaining stable solutions. This FALQON variant makes it suitable for the NISQ era.
